title: Hamilton's remarkable projects away from F1
excerpt:
This weekend’s Sao Paulo Grand Prix marks the 400th start for Lewis Hamilton in Formula 1. The seven-time World Champion has broken numerous records on track, including adding to his tally of 105 pole positions as recently as last weekend in Mexico, but is also one of racing's most influential personalities outside the paddock.

From his ventures in music and producing movies to being a co-chair during the 2025 Met Gala, Hamilton is a key figure in popular culture and has shown no signs of slowing down alongside his fast life in Formula 1. Here are some of the remarkable projects he has been involved with away from the track...

Rapping under a pseudonym

Hamilton has never shielded away from his love of creating music, even surprising fans with snippets of his songs during an Instagram Live broadcast in 2020. It received an excellent response, with several people begging for the champion to release a full album.

However, this wasn’t the first time we’d heard Hamilton on a track. Back in 2018, his friend Christina Aguilera released a song “Pipe” from her album Liberation featuring a mysterious guest artist, XNDA. Many had speculated that it sounded like Hamilton, but it was two years later when the driver of the #44 car confirmed his contribution to the track via an Instagram story.

“Guys, I've spent the last 10 years or more writing and recording, working with some of the most talented and beautiful people which I'm so grateful for,” Hamilton’s post said. “It's been the most incredible outlet. Finding something you love so much and can do just for you, for your spirit is I think such an important process.

"I've come to the place where I'd love to share it with you. I haven't got a project or album, just a bunch of different songs that perhaps some of you will be able to connect to. They have helped me get through some of the most difficult times. At some stage I'm going to find a moment to share with you so bare [sic] with me.

“I had this incredibly beautiful and talented person reach out to me a while back asking for me to be on her album. I was so blown away and I jumped at the opportunity. I had two hours to write the short verse and record.

"The goal was to have the music come out under a different name so that you could hear the music first and later know it was me but it didn't work out the way I'd planned. I shied away from acknowledging it was me, I don't know why, maybe insecurities, fear, overthinking, something I think many people can relate to.

“Well I want to say that XNDA is me and I am so honoured and grateful to Xtina for giving me a place to use my voice. I have so much gratitude and respect for her and what she's done in the business. #pipe”

Hamilton's incredible F1 records ahead of his 400th GP

Making appearances in video games

As well as the EA Sports F1 game, Hamilton can be found in several franchises: from Fortnite to Call of Duty.

The collaboration with Fortnite came in 2023, where users could play using their own playable skin of Hamilton. Sporting a colourful outfit and accompanied by his British bulldog Roscoe, who sadly passed away last year, Hamilton became a popular addition to the worldwide gaming phenomenon.

A decade ago, Hamilton also intercepted another gaming universe, with a cameo in the 2016 game Call of Duty: Infinite Warfare. Posing as Carl Hamilton, a nod to Lewis’ middle name, the character is an electro-technical engineer and crew member.

He joined the cast for the game alongside F1 fan and Game of Thrones actor Kit Harington and Baywatch and Knight Rider legend David Hasselhoff, and had to have his face scanned for the role.

Playing his cards right

Hamilton has turned his childhood passion for collecting trading cards into his latest business venture, opening his very own store earlier this year.

The seven-time World Champion launched Card Culture by Lewis Hamilton, a trading card business created in partnership with Dave & Adam's Card World. The first flagship store opened in Frankfurt, Germany, in July, with plans to expand to other locations across Europe, Australia, the Middle East and Asia.

Hamilton's love of collecting stretches back to his childhood, when he would trade football cards with friends at school. His personal interests in the hobby have since expanded to include other sports and popular culture.

The Briton has also become something of a collector's item himself, with a rare, one-of-a-kind autographed Topps card featuring Hamilton selling for more than $1 million in December 2024, becoming the first Formula 1 trading card to reach a seven-figure sum.

“I remember being in school and the excitement of opening up packs of cards - growing up in England it was mostly football - and then trading them with friends,” Hamilton told Sports Illustrated.

“It was a small community, but we were connected through our love of sport and cards.”

For Hamilton, the venture is about more than simply selling collectibles. He hopes to create spaces where enthusiasts can share their passion, while introducing a new generation to the hobby.

“I look at it as building a modern card store that mixes community, culture, and competition,” he explained.

How Lewis Hamilton became F1's most influential fashion icon

A respected face in fashion

Throughout his Formula 1 career, Hamilton has become known for his distinctive sense of style, regularly experimenting with clothing, jewellery and accessories to express his personality. His paddock entrances have attracted attention well beyond the world of motorsport, while helping to encourage other drivers to embrace fashion as a form of self-expression.

The Briton has long been a familiar face at fashion shows, even making a cameo appearance as himself in the 2016 comedy sequel* Zoolander 2*, but in recent years his involvement in the industry has reached new heights.

One of his most significant fashion moments came in May 2025, when Hamilton was selected as one of five co-chairs of the prestigious Met Gala, joining Colman Domingo, A$AP Rocky, Pharrell Williams and Anna Wintour.

Held annually at New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Met Gala raises funds for the museum's Costume Institute and celebrates the opening of its annual fashion exhibition. The 2025 exhibition, titled Superfine: Tailoring Black Style, explored the history and cultural significance of Black dandyism and its influence on fashion and identity.

To mark the occasion, Hamilton also appeared on the cover of Vogue's May 2025 issue, with the magazine releasing four special covers celebrating the event's co-chairs. Photographed by Malick Bodian, Hamilton wore a Ferragamo suit and off-white bow tie for the cover, further cementing his status as one of the sport's most recognisable figures in fashion.

Hamilton, who made his Met Gala debut in 2015, has also established partnerships with several major fashion brands, serving as a Dior menswear ambassador and guest designer, as well as becoming lululemon's inaugural motorsport ambassador.

Making his way into the movies

Another creative outlet for the seven-time champion is Hollywood. He has previously shared that some of his favourite films are Coming to America, Interstellar and *Ferris Bueller’s Day Off *– with Hamilton recreating the latter on his own social media last year.

His role as a producer – and briefly a cast member – for F1: The Movie has also served as a great source of education and enthusiasm for Hamilton, who has been very vocal about his love for director Joseph Kosinski.

“Coming on board to this project as a producer has been such an incredible learning process for me, seeing what goes into making a feature film, and there’s been a lot of learning on the other side too as everyone has got to grips with Formula 1,” Hamilton explained last year.

“I’ve always loved film and telling stories, and I’ve loved this sport since I was five years old, so when I got the opportunity to speak with Joe Kosinski and Jerry Bruckheimer about the project, it felt like the two worlds I’m passionate about coming together.

“I remember in the early days of the project I got to meet with Brad [Pitt] and go through the script, join meetings with the teams at Apple and Formula 1, and be part of some of the early casting processes. From those first conversations, to watching it all come together, it’s just been a super cool experience and I can’t wait for everyone to see it!”

Kosinski – who also directed Top Gun: Maverick – was apparently approached by Hamilton to appear in the showstopping fighter jet film. As a fan of the original like most of us, and his close friendship with Tom Cruise, it was believed that Hamilton asked them both for a part in the film when it was confirmed that a sequel was in the works.

Joking that he’d even be a “cleaner in the back and sweep something”, Hamilton was then given the green light and told he could be a pilot in the movie. Unfortunately for us F1 fans, Lewis described the “most upsetting call that I think I've ever had” in a GQ interview, where he had to turn down the opportunity due to clashes with the Formula 1 calendar.

title: Rivals pay tribute as Hamilton reaches 400 F1 starts
excerpt:
The Sao Paulo Grand Prix represents a milestone for Lewis Hamilton as the Ferrari driver reaches his 400th Formula 1 race this weekend.

It's a number only bettered by his former McLaren team mate Fernando Alonso, for whom Interlagos will be start number 445, but unlike Alonso, Hamilton hasn’t taken time out from F1, and thus his total reflects 20 continuous seasons of intense competition at the very top level.

Along the way he’s won the World Championship seven times, and logged 106 wins and 105 poles, adding to the latter total as recently as last weekend’s Mexico City Grand Prix.

That was further proof if anyone needed it that, at 41, Hamilton is still fully motivated and is still able to do what it takes to be competitive.

“It's kind of crazy,” he said at Interlagos on Thursday when asked about his 400th race. “I never ever thought that I would be reaching numbers like that. It's crazy, because I still feel young, and regardless of the things that people say, you saw my pole last week – I still have the pace, I still have the speed, and I still have the dedication, which is most important, and the focus.

“For me, that number is kind of irrelevant. It's beautiful to be able to have that here in Brazil. I've heard of some photographers who have been there for 500 races. At some stage, that's probably where I'll be.”

Alonso welcomes Hamilton as the second member of the ‘400 Club'

“Yes, of course,” said Alonso when asked about having Hamilton in the '400 Club'. “I think, yes, it's a big number. More and more drivers, I think, will join the club with these very long calendars. I think if you race 10 years now, you are more than 250.

“But yes, Lewis obviously has had an incredible career in F1, and 400 races, all of them in a very competitive position. Congratulations to him, and hopefully a good race and a good weekend for him.”

At 24 races a year, new World Champion Kimi Antonelli could join the '400 Club' as early as 2041.

It’s a happy co-incidence Interlagos is the Italian’s 44th start, a number so closely associated with someone who, along with Ayrton Senna, is one of his heroes.

“He's incredible,” said Antonelli. “First of all, how he can still perform at his age, like Fernando at the end of the day. To see him with the same hunger and determination is very cool, and inspirational as well. And it could be a good sign for me. I'm just 20, hopefully at 41, I'll be still here racing, and competing at the top.

“It's incredible what he has achieved. I mean, he has broken so many records and is still doing so. So very happy, and a big privilege to be able to race against him – and hopefully many more battles in the future.”

Antonelli’s Mercedes team mate George Russell spent three seasons racing alongside Hamilton, and he knows better than most just how good he is, and what makes him tick.

“What he's achieved on and off track has been incredible,” said Russell. “He's an inspiration to so many. The fact that he's not had a year off just shows the sort of character he is, and he is definitely built differently to a number of other athletes around the world. But that's why he's one of the best ever.

“He loves racing, he loves F1. He doesn't have much interest in other racing series outside of F1, because this is the pinnacle, and I respect that. I respect [Max] Verstappen on the other side, who's got a lot of interest in other racing series outside.

“There's no right or wrong, but he's still going strong. And this season has probably been his best season in F1 since 2021.”

Outgoing World Champion Lando Norris agrees that Hamilton’s form in 2026 has been impressive.

“It's pretty unbelievable, what he's been able to do for such a long time, even to now,” said Norris. “To see him fighting against Charles [Leclerc], and I think Charles is easily one of the best on the grid, insanely quick, and the fact that Lewis is still giving him a good fight, especially this year.

“I think everyone's enjoyed the fact he was able to give Charles a better performance, not just give his team mate a better performance, but also look like he was getting more out of the car, and achieving better results every time.

“He maybe seemed to not like the last few years as much in terms of the last few years of cars that we had, that kind of regulation. But he seems to look like he's back to normal in terms of fighting at the front, and proving that he's one of the best out there. So I think it's a pretty incredible achievement for him to fight for this long.”

Like so many of the younger generation, Norris is impressed by Hamilton’s career longevity.

“He's a good inspiration for many of us,” he said. “I certainly don't think I'm going that far, but it's a good thing to look forward to in terms of my career. I know I was happy with one championship. But when I look at Lewis, he makes me not very happy to have only won one championship!

“But that's in a good way, that I can look at him and see him at his age, in his form, and it makes me believe more than ever, that I can fight for many, many more years. And that's something I look forward to doing.”

title: What are the tyre strategy options for the Sao Paulo GP?
excerpt:
Lando Norris took P1 at Interlagos for the third year in a row, and is joined on the front row by Kimi Antonelli. But behind the front pair there’s an unusual look to the grid, with Liam Lawson and Nico Hulkenberg on row two, and Isack Hadjar and Ollie Bearman on row three.

The rest of the order is similarly topsy-turvy, in some instances because the wet-weather cream of the crop rose up the order in horrible conditions in Qualifying, but also because Max Verstappen, George Russell and both Ferrari drivers have elected to take tactical engine penalties here in Brazil.

It’s the right circuit to take the hit, given Interlagos is a good track for overtaking. It is frequently a multi-stop race, and it dispenses mayhem with predictably unpredictable frequency. The weather forecast is exciting, the top four teams are very closely matched on performance, and strategy is going to play a huge part today. Let the games begin!

title: Camara disappointed after crash in debut Qualifying
excerpt:
Rafael Camara says he is "disappointed" with his errors during an eventful Qualifying debut in difficult conditions at his home race in Sao Paulo, but feels "it was a positive session" overall.

Camara survived spinning and hitting the wall in pouring rain during Q1, before going off into the barrier to bring out the red flags in Q2, but qualified 13th fastest in his first F1 Qualifying session and will start the race from P11 due to grid penalties ahead of him.

The Brazilian rookie was unexpectedly put into the car this weekend after Esteban Ocon’s abrupt departure, having already been signed up for Haas next season.

Speaking after Qualifying, Camara said he was aiming for a clean race on Sunday.

The heavy rain and standing water on the track caused challenging conditions for all the drivers, something Camara said he struggled with. "That was a tricky one," he explained. "I'm okay. It was just a bit unlucky, I think, in the last corner, getting the lock-up and then after trying to release to make the corner, but it was really not possible.

"And yeah, in a way, [I'm] a bit disappointed with the mistakes. I know for the team it's not what they want, but overall I think it was a positive session.”

There is a chance Camara could score points on his F1 debut from where he starts on the grid, and he will have huge backing from his home crowd, but the 21-year-old says he just wants it to be incident free.

“We don't want to crash tomorrow," he said. "I think we just try to have a clean race, but I think the approach is just prepare as much as we can – go into the data, go to the engineers, and see what we can do best for tomorrow and make sure that we are ready for all the scenarios.

"I mean, there are a lot of things to do in the race, but [we will] just try to be as much ready as we can so we can do a good race.”

It was a good Qualifying session for his Haas teammate Ollie Bearman, who will line up in P6 on the grid.

The Briton survived an off-track moment of his own but ended up as one of the midfield drivers to benefit from the conditions, which mixed up the usual order, and grid penalties ahead promoted him even further.

“Yeah certainly a crazy session," he said. "I learned a lot from my first rodeo here two years ago, and I did a much better job. The team did a better job too on the wet tyre – when to push and when to cool.

"We did well, and it’s a shame about Q3. I think, compared to our competitors, we just struggled to put the tyres into the correct window, and I just didn’t have any grip. As soon as the rain came, it was game over.

"So yeah, I’m happy with the job we did. There’s a bit more out there, but that’s okay. We’ll get them tomorrow."

title: Russell rues ‘misjudgement’ that cost him Sao Paulo pole
excerpt:
A bittersweet Qualifying in Sao Paulo left George Russell feeling frustrated after a “misjudgement” cut his lap that “would’ve been good enough for pole” short, but his performance still gave him “confidence” for Sunday’s Grand Prix.

Nearly a week after he lost out on the Drivers’ Championship to his team mate Kimi Antonelli, Russell bounced back to fight for the top spot in Qualifying at Interlagos – a challenge that was made particularly difficult by torrential rain.

Despite the conditions, he mingled around the P1 slot on the timesheets before the weather worsened after the first Q3 runs. Assuming they’d get the chance to complete another lap, Mercedes told Russell to back off with Alex Albon just ahead, which proved to be the wrong call as his effort to that point was faster than polesitter Lando Norris’.

Elaborating on his subsequent flurry of irritated radio messages, he said: “Pole was ours for the taking there. It was just a misjudgement from us collectively as a team to abort my second lap.

“We thought we’d get another 60s without the rain – unfortunately, we got that wrong. That was a pole lap, I think. I got a bit held up by Albon, but it still would’ve been good enough for the pole.

“[The race is] going to be tricky, but it gives me confidence. It reminds me again that I’ve not forgotten how to drive, and I think that’s important in circumstances like these that I found myself in.

“It would’ve meant a lot to me to have clinched the pole with a great performance, like we showed in Qualifying. I think it kind of sums up this season.

“As a team, we’ve got one goal this weekend and that’s to seal the Constructors’. This season’s just very much not meant to be.”

Although Russell’s five-place grid penalty will demote him to P7, Mercedes will still be on course to score the three extra points they need to beat Ferrari to the Teams’ Championship, especially with Antonelli starting on the front row.

The Italian didn’t look as confident as Russell throughout Qualifying and wound up 0.625s adrift of Norris’ time, but moving up to P2 on the grid will put him in a strong position to add a 10th Grand Prix win to his tally.

“[It was] very difficult trying to understand this track in the wet,” Antonelli admitted. “It was [my] first time around here in the wet, and it just was not easy.

“Very slippery but I think in Q3 there was a lot more. I just made two big mistakes during the lap and that cost us the chance for a better position.

“I’m looking forward to [the race] if it’s wet. Obviously I have a lot more experience now with the car, so if it’s wet it’s going to be fun, but if it’s dry we’re going to do our best. I think overall there’s been big learning this session. Not how I wanted it to go, but still decent.”

title: What To Watch For in the Sao Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos
excerpt:
From Mercedes on the verge of another title to Max Verstappen chasing a hat-trick of recovery drives through the field, and from Ferrari also needing to recover from grid penalties to a new home hero chasing points on debut, here are just some of the areas you might want to keep an eye out for as we prepare for what is often an action-packed race at Interlagos.

1. Mercedes’ championship requirements

After Kimi Antonelli won the Drivers’ Championship last week in Mexico City, Mercedes can follow suit and secure the Constructors’ Championship themselves on Sunday.

The equation is a simple one: Mercedes need to outscore Ferrari by three points in the Sao Paulo Grand Prix to become champions, and they have a huge chance to do so given the grid penalties that both Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc are taking this weekend.

title: Hamilton reflects on grid penalties and PU changes in Brazil
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton admits that he was "using the Qualifying session as a test", with the Ferrari driver set to start at the back of the grid for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

The seven-time World Champion started Saturday in Brazil with a 10-place grid penalty, along with team mate Charles Leclerc, after both their cars had an Internal Combustion Engine (ICE) change.

But Hamilton suffered problems during Free Practice 3, with Ferrari forced to change more power unit elements ahead of Qualifying which resulted in further grid penalties.

Hamilton went out in the second part of a wet Qualifying, admitting that there was a lack of running in order to save tyres for a potentially wet 71-lap race on Sunday.

"It was a lot of fun out there. It's always fun in the rain. It's very, very tricky, but I had just a lot of fun, just in the few laps that we got," said Hamilton.

"I wish I was still out there battling with the guys, but unfortunately, saving the tyres for tomorrow."

"That's what we're trying to do, yeah," said Hamilton when asked if a charge through the field from P20 was possible.

"It's going to be really tricky conditions, but I love racing in the rain. I was basically using the Qualifying session as a test in making sure the engine is working and making sure that the car felt good, so I feel good for tomorrow."

Leclerc managed to reach the final part of Qualifying and finished fourth fastest, which will be converted to a P14 start after his penalty is applied.

Having claimed to have "learnt a huge amount today" during the wet weather running, the Monegasque driver was hopeful of reaching the podium with a climb through the field.

"I'm feeling good, I'm looking forward to it," said Leclerc. "We knew taking an engine penalty here, we knew that everything is to play for still because you've got crazy weather all the time.

"It's good to see that the weather is still crazy for tomorrow and hopefully that will give us an opportunity to come back on the podium from where we start."

title: Sao Paulo GP starting grid heavily adjusted after severe Lewis Hamilton, Max Verstappen penalties
excerpt:
Two further changes have been announced to the grid for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, with Arvid Lindblad and Gabriel Bortoleto being demoted to 18th and 19th following 10-place penalties each.

Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen are to start at Interlagos from 20th and 21st, respectively, after major engine penalties. Lindblad and Bortoleto's penalties are also due to engine component changes.

The two world champions knew they would be starting at the back heading into the treacherous qualifying, after taking new power units - which, in Hamilton's case, was the second of the weekend after his initial new engine sprung a problem in FP3.

They both fell in Q2, although they did not make an attempt to reach Q3, which was topped by fellow world champion Lando Norris, who sailed to pole position.

The outgoing champion is joined on the front row by the incoming one, Kimi Antonelli, after George Russell's second on the road became seventh after his own penalty.

Liam Lawson equalled his career-best grid spot with third, having been fifth on the road before the penalties for Russell and Charles Leclerc, who was fourth, and drops to P14.

title: Two further F1 drivers handed penalties in crazy Sao Paulo GP grid
excerpt:
Two further drivers have been handed grid penalties for the São Paulo Grand Prix, further shaking up what is already a crazy grid at Interlagos.

Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad has received a 10-place grid penalty after a new internal combustion engine and turbocharger were fitted to his car, both of which are outside his legal pool.

As a result, the Briton will start 18th on the grid, one position ahead of Gabriel Bortoleto in 19th, who is the second driver to receive a grid drop.

Bortoleto's Audi has been fitted with a new energy store and control electronics unit. Both components are also outside his legal allocation.

The home driver has received a 10-place grid penalty, dropping him to 19th, ahead of Lewis Hamilton, Max Verstappen and Sergio Perez, who all have major grid drops following extensive power unit component changes.

title: Charles Leclerc surprise after nine-year Ferrari 'biggest weakness' progress
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc admitted surprise after finally finding a Ferrari that worked for him in the wet, insisting it was the first time in nine years at Maranello that rain had not exposed the car's "biggest weakness".

The Monegasque qualified fourth for the São Paulo Grand Prix, carrying a 10-place grid penalty that will drop him well down the order for Sunday's race at Interlagos.

Lewis Hamilton, his Ferrari team-mate, could only manage 11th as changeable conditions at Interlagos shuffled the order throughout Saturday's session although he starts from 20th due to his own penalty.

Despite the penalty rendering his grid slot largely academic, Leclerc said the wet qualifying session had value beyond the result itself, with Ferrari using the compromised weekend to test experimental set-up direction.

Discussing how a top three finish in qualifying would have been better than the fourth place he actually took, Leclerc told select media, including RacingNews365: "Yeah. However, it's a very strange feeling because, of course, I'm not happy with P4, and I think the end result is a little bit disappointing.

"However, I believe that this has been a very, very interesting session and a session where we've learnt and that we will learn a lot from going forward."

"Having the 10-place grid penalty, I think we allowed ourselves to be a bit more experimental on various different things, and I think there was a very good correlation between where we were strong during this session and where we were not strong, and what we were doing in the background. So I think it's going to be very helpful going forward."

Unexpected Ferrari wet weather positives

Leclerc has long cited wet conditions as an area where Ferrari has lagged behind its rivals since he joined the team in 2019, a struggle he contrasted sharply with his own junior career form in the rain.

"In nine years with the team, I think the weakness, and the biggest weakness, I think, has always been wet sessions in general," said Leclerc.

"Whereas, in the junior categories, that was probably my biggest strength. There were moments in qualifying when I had a very good feeling with the car.

"Unfortunately, we didn't do a good job in Q3, but that doesn't matter too much to me because starting 11th, 12th, 13th or 14th, honestly, it's not a big change."

title: F1 drivers face major Sao Paulo GP headache after weather surprise
excerpt:
Rain was feared by many for race day in Interlagos, but it might just end up an entirely dry São Paulo Grand Prix.

Rain remains a genuine threat for the São Paulo Grand Prix, but a dry race is far from off the table. Should Interlagos stay dry, the grid faces an entirely different challenge when it comes to tyre strategy.

Qualifying for the race was held in treacherous conditions, a session that proved brutal for Gabriel Bortoleto and Rafael Câmara in particular. But the wet session has also left every driver with a markedly different tyre allocation heading into the race.

All 22 drivers go into Sunday with a healthy stock of fresh slick tyres. Those who reached Q3 carry only a minimal, almost negligible disadvantage, with four sets of fresh soft tyres compared to five for everyone eliminated earlier in qualifying. Every driver also has one fresh set of mediums and one fresh set of hards in hand.

Should the race switch to wet conditions, the picture around available sets shifts again, though not dramatically in anyone's favour.

Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton would head into any potential recovery drive with five fresh sets of intermediates at their disposal. By contrast, Lando Norris and George Russell have only two sets left, while Kimi Antonelli has three.

Should intermediates be needed, the key question becomes how quickly they degrade on a wet track. If that wear turns out to be significant, it could hand Verstappen and Hamilton a genuine advantage.

According to the forecast, the rain does not appear heavy enough to bring full wet tyres into play.

Article continues below the image...

Cooler temperatures add extra unknown Brazil element

Even if it stays completely dry, there is still the question of how the tyres behave in conditions that are far cooler than those seen in practice.

Third practice, for example, was run in temperatures of 26 to 27 degrees. Sunday's forecast tops out at no more than 15 degrees, a difference that makes a considerable impact.

The tyres are likely to wear less overall, but other factors come into play, graining among them. Pirelli has indicated that a two-stop strategy will be the quickest route to the flag, while also outlining several alternatives. The question is whether the colder temperatures could upset that calculation.

Making a two-stop work requires drivers to push hard throughout each stint. That pushing causes the core temperature of the tyre to rise quickly, but the cold asphalt and air keep the outer rubber comparatively cool and stiff.

That sharp temperature difference causes problems in the corners: the softer inner layer flexes while the stiffer outer layer is dragged out of shape. The result is graining, a roughening of the tyre surface that brings a rapid loss of grip.

The opposite scenario carries its own risks. A one-stop strategy, or leaning on the harder compounds, brings the danger of over-managing the tyres to the point where both the core and the outer layer cool down and drop out of their working window.

That leaves the car sliding more than usual. Once cold tyres are asked to cope with lateral loads through the corners, the rubber fails to "bite" into the tarmac, and grip disappears rapidly.

A dry race would leave the field facing a grand prix full of unknowns over tyre behaviour and the ideal strategy. Whether Brazil ultimately serves up a dry race, a wet one, or something in between remains the biggest unknown of all heading into Sunday.

title: Oscar Piastri addresses red flag impact after shock early qualifying exit
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri has played down suggestions that a late red flag cost him a place in Q3 at Interlagos, insisting his Q2 elimination in Brazil came down to tyre choice and timing rather than bad luck.

The McLaren driver was eliminated in 12th place in a rain-hit qualifying session at the São Paulo Grand Prix, well adrift of team-mate Lando Norris, who took pole position with a 1m 27.470s lap.

Piastri's best effort of 1m 30.369s left him more than two tenths outside the top 10 as conditions shifted from wet to intermediate tyres during the session.

Q2 was red-flagged with around 45 seconds remaining after Rafael Camara crashed his Haas at the final real braking zone, denying several drivers, including Piastri, the chance to complete a final improving lap.

Reflecting on the session, Piastri admitted McLaren may have left the switch to inters too late.

"I just finished a lap, but I think we probably went onto the inters a little bit too late and needed that extra lap or two to really get some temperature in them," Piastri told select media, including RacingNews365.

"Some of the lines I was using on the wets definitely didn't work on the inters. So, yeah, some things to review, of course.

"But yeah, I think with another lap and maybe slightly better decisions, we could have been there [in Q3]."

Oscar Piastri hopeful of dry São Paulo GP

Pressed on whether the red flag itself was to blame for his early exit, Piastri was reluctant to point the finger at the timing of Camara's crash.

Asked to clarify whether he was blaming the red flag for his exit, Piastri replied: "I definitely would have got one more lap in. But, you know, same for everybody.

"Everyone would have got another lap, so I'm not sure. I think there was definitely a lot more time out there. But yeah, you just need to be on the right tyre at the right time."

Looking ahead to the race, the Australian said he felt comfortable with McLaren's pace in dry conditions over the weekend, regardless of what the forecast brings for Sunday.

Discussing if a wet or dry race would best suit him, Piastri said: "I'm not sure. I think we looked good in the dry. I certainly felt pretty comfortable this weekend.

"I feel like things were going well. So yeah, wait and see what we get. I think if it's dry, then we've got a good baseline. But we'll have to wait and see."

title: George Russell issues Mercedes engineer defence after 'wrong decision' frustration
excerpt:
George Russell was fired up after Brazil qualifying but has stressed his engineer was not to blame.

George Russell has defended his Mercedes race engineer after being told to abort a flying lap in Q3 for the São Paulo Grand Prix, only for heavier rain to arrive moments later and deny the Briton a shot at pole position.

Russell ended up second in qualifying at Interlagos, 0.204s off Lando Norris's benchmark of 1m 27.470, but will start the race down in seventh after a grid penalty.

Toto Wolff intervened directly on his driver's radio during the session as frustration boiled over on the Mercedes pit wall.

The 28-year-old had been flying before the call to back off came through, with his engineer telling him to ease up after catching Alex Albon's Williams on track, just as the rain intensified.

Speaking after qualifying, Russell said he believed another lap was possible before the rain arrived.

"Yeah, I think it was just a bit of miscommunication," said Russell. "I need to speak with the team because we believed we'd get another lap before the rain came in.

"So, I was on a really strong lap and I was asked to back off because I caught up with Albon, and then obviously the rain came. So yeah, it was very disappointing.

"Need to understand how it happened and why we got that wrong. But I felt very strong the whole session. Similar to Lando, I had more confidence in the wet than I had in the dry. But yeah, definitely felt pole was there for the taking."

Driver

George Russell

63

George Russell not pointing finger at race engineer

The Mercedes driver made clear he did not blame the man on the other end of his radio for the call, pointing instead to the wider decision-making process behind it.

"They've got the weather forecast in front of them and I don't," added Russell. "And, you know, this is where you need that trust and you're relying on one another.

"Obviously, it was the wrong decision, and it was a decision that I think as soon as it was made, I think we knew it was the wrong one because already they could actually feel the rain pouring harder.

"So, we need to understand, you know, we're relying on a lot of systems, and we can't point the finger at somebody. We need to understand why we made that decision and whether our systems were telling us what we needed to know, because you're relying on the radar.

"But it doesn't make it any less frustrating for me, and it's not my engineer's fault. He's relaying information. He's ultimately the one who passes the message on, but he's got 12 people talking to him, giving him that information to relay on. So, we just need to understand why we made that decision."

title: Kimi Antonelli to 'frame' Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen after 'special moment'
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has revealed he will frame the picture of Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton lifting him onto their shoulders on the Mexico City podium as one of the most :special moments" of his career.

The 20-year-old sealed the 2026 drivers' title with third place at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, a result that mathematically ended the title fight with four rounds still to run.

Verstappen and Hamilton, who finished first and second respectively, hoisted the new champion onto their shoulders on the podium in a spontaneous show of celebration.

Antonelli's triumph came in his second season with Mercedes rather than as a rookie, following his debut campaign in 2025. He is the youngest world champion in F1 history.

Speaking on the Nu Silver Arrows radio show, Antonelli said the gesture from two of the sport's most decorated drivers left him overwhelmed.

"Yeah, it's surreal," began Antonelli. "I'm very grateful for all the opportunities that I have been given, and this moment, the moment on the podium, is one of those memories that will live forever.

"First of all, to see so much respect and appreciation from the two drivers who have made the history of the sport, and they're still doing so because they're still competing at the top and achieving incredible results," he said.

"To see so much respect and appreciation, and for sure, what they did, picking me up on the podium, is a moment that I will always be grateful to them for as well, because it was also unexpected for me.

"Once they picked me up, I was just so happy and I got so emotional as well, because it was such a special moment for me. And definitely, that picture, I will frame it, as I said many times. I will frame it and put it on the wall because it's such a special memory and such a special moment that will always be remembered."

Mexico City photo 'one of the most special' of Antonelli's career

Radio show host for the episode, former F1 driver Anthony Davidson, compared the photograph to images of Ayrton Senna, Alain Prost and Nigel Mansell, three drivers he grew up watching.

Asked whether the image could stand alongside famous podium photographs from that era, Antonelli placed it among his own most treasured memories.

"I mean for sure it's a very special one," added Antonelli.

"I think for me, like among with Monza, it's probably one of the most special pictures that I've ever seen from my side, of course. Like pictures of course, from my racing career."

title: What is greatest Lewis Hamilton F1 victory ahead of landmark 400th start?
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton is poised to make his 400th Formula 1 start this weekend at Interlagos, arriving at the São Paulo Grand Prix on the back of 399 race starts, 106 wins and seven world championships.

The milestone places the Ferrari driver among a tiny group of drivers to reach the mark, with Fernando Alonso the first to pass 400 grand prix weekends back in 2024. Hamilton has long sat as the nearest active driver to that landmark.

Across two decades, Hamilton has built a body of victories that spans conditions, teams and eras, from a rain-soaked Silverstone masterclass as a youngster to a tyre-management triumph that sealed a record-equalling seventh title. Choosing a single standout is no simple task.

The 2008 British Grand Prix saw Hamilton dominate in torrential rain and standing water that sent much of the field spinning off. In São Paulo in 2021, he recovered from a qualifying disqualification and further grid penalties to win from 10th on the grid, overhauling Max Verstappen along the way.

The 2020 Turkish Grand Prix brought one of his most technically accomplished drives, nursing a single set of intermediates for 50 laps on a drying track to clinch title number seven.

Germany in 2018 combined a 14th-place qualifying disaster with a late safety car and a bold pit-lane recovery to snatch victory from Sebastian Vettel's misfortune.

And the 2024 British Grand Prix ended a 945-day winless run, with Hamilton in tears on his slow-down lap and a ninth Silverstone triumph that stands as the most wins by any driver at a single circuit.

With a potential milestone 2026 Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix also in the mix, RacingNews365 wants to know which of these drives you rate as Hamilton's finest.

What is Hamilton's greatest F1 victory? Have your say by voting in the poll below!

title: Ralf Schumacher issues brutal Colton Herta criticism: 'Just burning fuel'
excerpt:
Ralf Schumacher has delivered a scathing verdict on Colton Herta's chances of landing Cadillac's second seat for 2027, dismissing the American's prospects out of hand.

Herta took to the track for Cadillac again during first practice in Sao Paulo, his sixth outing of the season as the squad's reserve driver.

The 26-year-old stood in for Sergio Perez, who has already extended his own deal with the American manufacturer through 2029.

Herta completed over 24 laps which meant he finally moved to 40 points on his superlicence, enough to race in F1 should Cadillac offer him Valtteri Bottas' seat.

Asked whether he hoped to land a full-time race seat for 2027, Herta told Sky Sports in Brazil that the goal remains firmly on his radar.

"That is of course my goal. That's why I'm here and that's why I'm giving so much for it. I hope that it happens."

Colton Herta 'has no business' in F1 - Ralf Schumacher

But Ralf Schumacher, working as a pundit for Sky DE, does not rate Herta's prospects at all.

"Only if Easter and Christmas fall on the same day. No, honestly, it's pointless," insisted Schumacher.

"He's just burning fuel, as Franz Tost [the long-time F1 team principal] would say. I don't even know what the point is. You could put other people, young people, in the car instead.

"Herta was really, really bad in Formula 2. For me, he hasn't earned this at all."

Herta is in his first season in Formula 2 having made his name in IndyCar, but results have been underwhelming.

After 12 race weekends he sits just 19th in the standings on 26 points, hardly the form to strengthen a Formula 1 case.

"I think it's nice that they're trying to push an American driver. But it has to make sense, and he has no business being in Formula 1," added Schumacher.

As for who Schumacher would put in the Cadillac instead, the German pointed to a current McLaren reserve driver as a far stronger candidate.

"Leonardo Fornaroli is certainly a candidate who would deserve the chance too," he said. "He became Formula 2 and Formula 3 champion after all. An absolutely strong guy."

title: Toto Wolff makes remarkable Kimi Antonelli claim: 'He wouldn't have lasted'
excerpt:
Toto Wolff believes Kimi Antonelli would likely have been dropped by a rival team had he endured his torrid 2025 spell anywhere other than Mercedes.

The Mercedes team principal made the remarkable claim while reflecting on Antonelli's journey to F1 champion, which included a nine-race run of grands prix in Europe last season in which he scored a miserable three points.

The 20-year-old Italian arrived in F1 off the back of a F2 campaign with Prema in which he finished sixth, hardly a dominant platform typically demanded of a direct graduate into a frontline factory seat.

Mercedes bypassed the conventional route of blooding Antonelli at another team, the kind of pathway Red Bull and Ferrari have used with programmes such as Racing Bulls and Haas, instead throwing him straight into the deep end.

That decision came under pressure as the 2025 season unfolded and Antonelli struggled for results and performances.

Wolff, though, maintained faith in his young star, yielding his astonishing charge this year to becoming the youngest F1 champion in the sport's history.

After a few days to allow the enormity of Antonelli's success to sink in, speaking to Sky Sports F1, he said: "The week was good.

"You realised that we won the championship with a very special young man. It was a positive week mindset.

"I wake up in the morning, and I'm thinking that was a good one."

[Article continues below]

Wolff then turned to the scrutiny Antonelli faced during his difficult run last season, crediting the team's approach for keeping him in the car.

"What I'm particularly proud of is that I don't think he would have lasted in other teams after an F2 season, which wasn't overwhelming, and this spell of nine races without any points [sic] last year," Wolff said.

"We trusted our data, trusted our feeling about the personality and the potential, because there are so many who have come out now and said, 'What a talent!', and that wasn't the journey.

"The journey was developing the talent, nurturing, mentoring, shielding him, protecting him, and eventually he and the car just delivered absolutely amazingly."

title: Why Lewis Hamilton starts ahead of Max Verstappen despite bigger penalty explained
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton picked up a grand total of 75 places in grid penalties for the São Paulo Grand Prix, while Max Verstappen was hit with 30. Yet the Ferrari driver will still line up ahead of the Red Bull driver on Sunday.

Ferrari had initially planned only to swap the internal combustion engine on Hamilton's SF-26, a change that would have cost him 10 grid places.

But a problem with the power unit emerged during third practice, prompting the Scuderia to fit the seven-time champion with an entirely fresh engine. That resulted in a 65-place penalty, taking his total to 75.

Verstappen already knew before qualifying at Interlagos that there was little left to play for. The Dutchman also took on new power unit components, leaving him with a 30-place grid penalty.

Hamilton ended up 11th in qualifying, while Verstappen opted to sit out Q2 to save wet-weather tyres for the race, finishing 16th as a result.

The exact rule behind Hamilton-Verstappen starting positions

Despite Hamilton's penalty dwarfing that of Verstappen, the Briton will still start ahead of the Milton Keynes-based outfit's driver. The regulations draw a line between penalties of 15 places or fewer and penalties exceeding 15 places.

When the starting order is worked out, drivers with penalties of 15 places or fewer are slotted onto the grid first.

George Russell, for example, received a five-place penalty for new power unit parts, dropping him from second to seventh. Charles Leclerc fell from fourth to 14th for the same reason, having been hit with a 10-place penalty.

After those adjustments, every driver without a penalty is placed on the grid, filling in the gaps left behind by the drivers serving penalties of 15 places or fewer.

Only then do the drivers with penalties exceeding 15 places get dealt with. Article B2.5.4.b.iv of the sporting regulations comes into play at that point: every driver with a penalty of more than 15 places is sent to the back of the field.

Whoever qualified highest among them gets the best remaining position, with the actual number of places above 15 becoming irrelevant. Since Hamilton qualified 11th and Verstappen 16th, the Ferrari driver takes the higher spot.

The same rule explains why Sergio Pérez will start last despite a 30-place penalty of his own. The Cadillac driver qualified 21st.

title: Sunday morning Brazil F1 weather update as rain threat remains
excerpt:
Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton could do with some rain at Interlagos after both being handed grid penalties that send the duo to the back of the São Paulo Grand Prix grid.

Hamilton starts 20th, with Verstappen in 21st, after both drivers took several new engine components outside their respective pools, setting up an exciting fight back through the field.

Lando Norris claimed pole position, ahead of Kimi Antonelli and a surprising Liam Lawson in third. To add to the shocks, Audi's Nico Hulkenberg starts fourth.

George Russell set the second-fastest time but will also drop five places on the grid to seventh following an internal combustion engine change.

Just like in qualifying, wet weather remains a real threat for the grand prix, with rain expected throughout the day at Interlagos.

Rain continued to fall steadily throughout the night at the circuit and is expected to intensify during the morning before becoming lighter in the afternoon.

The heavy downpours and thunderstorms of Saturday are not expected to be a factor on race day, as the rain is set to remain lighter but consistent.

Current forecasts suggest the rain will be at its heaviest between 9am and noon in Interlagos, before returning to a lighter state for the race.

Major temperature fall

However, as was proven in qualifying, the weather can change in a split second at the legendary venue, where the temperature is set to fall dramatically.

The temperature swing compared to Saturday is striking. While the mercury reached 29 to 30 degrees Celsius during qualifying, Sunday's race is expected to stay below 15 degrees.

This creates the possibility of a cold, wet and chaotic grand prix, where tyre warm-up could prove extremely challenging.

All the challenges ahead do at least open the door to comeback drives from Verstappen and Hamilton.

title: Fernando Alonso faced ‘unreachable planet’ in Aston Martin F1 breakthrough
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has described how the top six cars in the dreadful Sao Paulo Grand Prix qualifying conditions were on an "unreachable planet."

For the first time in 2026, Alonso put the Aston Martin into Q3 in qualifying in the dreadful conditions of Interlagos, with the two-time champion taking ninth on the road, behind Haas's Oliver Bearman and ahead of the Williams of Alex Albon.

However, he will be promoted to eighth on the grid following Charles Leclerc's 10-place penalty for an engine change, which drops him from fourth to 14th.

Despite the Aston Martin having its most competitive session of the season in the rain, Alonso was not able to beat Bearman, who was 0.480s quicker in Q3.

Aside from Bearman, Isack Hadjar was seventh on the road and was 1.548s quicker than Alonso's best Q3 lap of 1:30.311, with Liam Lawson's Racing Bulls machine 1.990s quicker than Alonso in fifth on the road, which will be third on the grid for the New Zealander.

Alonso did not think it was possible to match those ahead, whom he described as being as on an "unreachable planet."

"It was on the limit, but it was better than waiting in the garage, and I was thinking, and it depended on the rain intensity, but I was thinking that maybe the top five was possible," Alonso reflected to media, including RacingNews365.

"The tyres had no grip on lap one, so I said: 'Okay, I will push on lap two, but the energy modes spent a lot of energy on lap one, so I didn't have full energy on lap two, so I ended up in no man's land.

"Lap one was not optimised for the tyres, lap two not for the engine, and I think there was maybe half-a-second or eight tenths of a second of performance to unlock in Q3.

"But when I see the times, that would only offer me one position, so I think the top six guys were on an unreachable planet."

Reflecting further on his session, Alonso detailed how his tyres were "ice cold" in Q3.

"Circumstances open a new opportunity for people at the back, and we took some risks in Q1 and Q2 where the conditions were an unknown for everybody," he said.

"It was the first Q3 of the year, but then in Q3, I was expecting more, but I was the first in the queue and the tyres were ice cold, so I had no grip.

"P6 was 1.8s in front of me, so it was too much to dream about any higher places."

[Article continues below]

Alonso offers Honda assessment

With the wet conditions known as a great leveller of car performance, Alonso felt that the power deficit he has with the Honda compared to other units was nullified, but that outright power was not the most important factor.

"Obviously, there is less time on full throttle because there is no grip, so they cannot exploit the extra power," Alonso added, referring to his power deficit compared to rivals.

"But the engine is still very important in terms of drivability and the way it behaves in the corners, and we still have a bit of an issue there, but these conditions are more about the level of risk you want to take.

"There is a little bit of aquaplaning here and there, and you want to make it through in the top 15 first, and then in the top 10 secondly, and you just try to level the risk just to make it through."

Turning to his hopes for the race, Alonso hoped it would continue to rain to allow the team to score points.

"Between the low visibility and the tricky race, wet conditions will offer us a bit better chance to score points," he said.

"I think in dry conditions there is no way. We were P18 this morning in FP3, so we are struggling a little bit more than expected here, so maybe wet conditions will help us."

title: Charles Leclerc acknowledges Lewis Hamilton 'tension' in Ferrari supremacy fight
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has admitted to “tension” between himself and Lewis Hamilton this year, which came to a head in Mexico City last week.

The pair battled for the lead on the opening lap but ran off the track to give an advantage to Max Verstappen, who went on to win the race.

Ahead of the following round in Sao Paulo, both drivers discussed the matter after Leclerc travelled to Interlagos following the birth of his first child.

Both drivers have insisted that the subject is a closed door as they look to enjoy a successful end to the year.

When asked how he felt the meeting went with Hamilton, Leclerc told media including RacingNews365: “From my perspective, I was very straightforward.

“It was good to speak. This is always needed after a moment like this. It took proportions that are way too big, but it has been around for way too long.

“At the same time, it was a very special week for me, so I couldn't really have those discussions before.

“It was important to have those discussions, but now I consider that a closed chapter, and I think it would be important to look ahead.”

[Article continues below]

Hamilton and Leclerc have been closely matched this year, a much different story compared to last year when Hamilton struggled to get up to speed at his new team.

The battle has generated “tension”, Leclerc admitted, but nothing that wasn't able to be ironed out by discussing such concerns.

“I really believe that when we speak, things are much better straight away,” he said.

“Of course there is tension, of course, we want to finish ahead of each other.

“Sometimes we are not going to do things right. It's okay sometimes to disagree on the way you see things.

“But at the same time, discussing those [things] then helps a whole lot.”

title: Toto Wolff bursts George Russell bubble after Brazil qualifying fury
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has stated it was unlikely George Russell would have taken the fastest lap in Q3 after the Mercedes driver voiced his anger over team radio at the end of the session.

Russell was heard venting his fury when heavy rainfall arrived late in the session, just after he was told to back off his previous lap as he was closing in on the back of Alex Albon.

The Mercedes driver was adamant that it would have put him in front of Lando Norris in the final classification, with the latter securing his third pole in three years at Interlagos.

However, Wolff was unconvinced that Russell would have been able to set a time to beat Norris as he got ever nearer to Albon.

"If we were to have a crystal ball to know whether you should back off or not, that would be helpful," he told Sky F1.

"It was a difficult one, a 50-50 call. He was running into Albon.

"He was 18 milliseconds up on Norris at that stage. I don't think it would have been enough for pole, but he drove perfectly all session and merited to be on pole."

Had Russell ended Q3 with the fastest lap time, he would not have been credited with pole position, as he takes a five-place grid penalty into Sunday's race.

He is now set to start from seventh, but Wolff insisted the Briton was the star performer from the session.

"He deserved it, but you can't make that call," he said. "It's 50 per cent right or wrong.

"George was in a league of his own today."
